==========================================================================
LAB 64.2 --- THE FOUR QUESTIONS, AND WHAT THEIR ANSWERS ARE WORTH
==========================================================================

Ask them first. They cost a conversation, not a login, and nothing
else you can do is that cheap. Then read the answers for what they
are: evidence with a weight, not a verdict with a name.

Before any question is asked, 10 causes are in play and
3.17 bits of the answer are missing.

CASE A --- everything is slow, since a push at 09:10
----------------------------------------------------
  did it ever work?  yes, then stopped
  is it one or many? everywhere
  what changed?      a change 15 minutes either side, in an estate making 40 changes a day
  when exactly?      close enough to that change to correlate

  That correlation is worth a likelihood ratio of 1.77, or 0.82 bits:
  an unrelated change lands in the same window 56.5% of the time anyway.
  It moves "this was change-triggered" from 70% to 80.5%, and the
  hypotheses below are reweighted by exactly that much and no more.

  RANKED HYPOTHESES (uncertainty remaining: 2.33 bits of a possible 3.32)
       38.3%  shared_service    a shared service (name resolution, address assignment, authentication)
       21.0%  config_error      a configuration or design error on the path
       14.1%  capacity          congestion --- the path works but not at this rate
       13.5%  filter_selective  a filter or policy that matches only some traffic
        8.7%  path_partial      one broken member of a bundle, or an MTU mismatch on one path

  WHAT THESE ANSWERS DID NOT RULE OUT: 6 of 10 causes still carry
  at least one per cent. Among them:
       14.1%  capacity          congestion --- the path works but not at this rate
       13.5%  filter_selective  a filter or policy that matches only some traffic
        8.7%  path_partial      one broken member of a bundle, or an MTU mismatch on one path
        3.3%  hardware_silent   forwarding hardware that drops while the control plane looks right

  TESTS, BY WHAT THEY WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE
      0.52 bits  test the address rather than the name
                  ("the address works and the name does not" 36% likely before you run it)
      0.24 bits  pin the flow to each bundle member in turn
                  ("one member fails while the others pass" 15% likely before you run it)
      0.13 bits  compare the programmed entry with the route (Lab 64.3)
                  ("what is programmed disagrees with what is routed" 7% likely before you run it)
      0.12 bits  full-size packets with fragmentation forbidden
                  ("large packets fail where small ones pass" 12% likely before you run it)
      and last, at 0.05 bits: another host on the same wall port

  Run the first one and you land on shared_service at 90.6% if it
  passes, or config_error at 31.2% if it fails. Either way you have 0.52 bits
  more than the questionnaire gave you, for the price of one test.

HOW MUCH "IT CORRELATES WITH A CHANGE" IS WORTH
----------------------------------------------
  changes/day   coincidence   likelihood ratio   bits   70% becomes
            2         4.1%              24.50   4.61        98.3%
           10        18.8%               5.32   2.41        92.5%
           40        56.5%               1.77   0.82        80.5%
          100        87.5%               1.14   0.19        72.7%
          200        98.4%               1.02   0.02        70.3%
          500       100.0%               1.00   0.00        70.0%

  Past 33 changes a day, a +/-15-minute correlation is worth
  less than a likelihood ratio of 2 --- which is to say, less than
  one bit. The estate that automates hardest is the estate where
  "it started right after the change" stops meaning anything, and
  it is the estate most likely to say it with confidence.

DOES ANY OF THIS SURVIVE CHANGING THE NUMBERS THIS LAB MADE UP?
--------------------------------------------------------------
  Sweeping the prior on a configuration error, and re-asking whether
  "never worked, one user" establishes one:

    prior on config error   posterior   does it establish it?
                   2.0%        1.6%   no
                  10.0%        8.3%   no
                  18.0%       15.2%   no
                  26.0%       22.3%   no
                  34.0%       29.7%   no
                  42.0%       37.2%   no
                  50.0%       45.0%   no
                  58.0%       53.0%   YES --- the claim fails here
                  66.0%       61.4%   YES --- the claim fails here
                  74.0%       70.0%   YES --- the claim fails here
                  82.0%       78.8%   YES --- the claim fails here
                  90.0%       88.0%   YES --- the claim fails here

  The claim holds at 7 of 12 settings and fails at the
  remaining 5. The crossing is at a prior of 55.0%: if you
  believe beforehand that configuration errors cause more than
  55% of all faults, then "never worked, one user" does
  establish one --- but the questionnaire is no longer telling you
  that, your prior is. That is the assumption the original made
  without writing it down, and this is the honest shape of the
  result: a claim with a stated range, not a claim.

WHAT TO DO WITH THE ANSWERS
---------------------------
  Ask the four questions first; they are still the cheapest thing on
  the list. Write down what they leave alive, not just what they
  favour. Then pick the test that separates your top two, and if no
  test separates them, you have not got two hypotheses --- you have
  got one hypothesis and a spare. The questionnaire ranks. Only a
  test decides.
